rows.why: AI tools, browser extensions, local models, agent frameworks and MCP software staff adopted without approval are identified and recorded in the inventory with where each came from.
Controls that stop staff installing or reaching unvetted AI (software safelists, blocked AI services, restricted AI browser extensions) are identified and documented.

For each unapproved AI tool, extension or local model found, the likelihood and severity of its impact (data it can reach, privileges it runs with, public incident reports) are rated to set the order of treatment.
Staff are regularly engaged to surface the AI tools and experiments they use and the needs behind them, so unseen use and its impacts come to light.
Endpoints, network traffic and logs are monitored continuously to detect new unapproved AI tools, local model runners and agent or MCP software as they appear.
AI tools, browser extensions, local model runtimes and MCP or agent packages staff installed from unvetted public sources are checked for malicious code and known vulnerabilities.
Use of unapproved AI services and locally installed AI software is logged and attributable to the person, so what was used and when can be traced and reviewed.
The risk of personal and sensitive data leaving through unapproved AI tools is examined, including checks on data sent to public AI services.
For each AI tool or experiment found in unapproved use, a decision is made whether it serves a real purpose and is brought under approval and support, or must stop.
Access staff can grant to AI tools (OAuth consents, tokens, delegated permissions running with their privileges) is controlled, centralised and reviewed for excess.
Unapproved AI software can be removed or blocked, and the access staff granted to AI tools is revoked when they leave or change role.
Incidents from unapproved AI use, such as data pasted into a public AI service, are reported, tracked, responded to and reviewed.
